confounds: The dataset is imbalanced: 618 diagnosed users versus 5,463 controls, so rare-feature estimates have substantial uncertainty despite the large total sample.
Clinical, treatment, and diagnostic terms may be annotation or ascertainment leakage rather than independent linguistic correlates.

No demographic, age, gender, platform, or sampling metadata are available. Sexual-language prevalence was also higher among diagnosed users (62.6% vs 48.9%), suggesting possible demographic or collection confounding rather than a depression mechanism.
Source order is available but timestamps are not; repeated posts measure within-timeline recurrence, not calendar persistence or symptom duration.
Portuguese slang, profanity, negation, quotation, lyric/media discussion, jokes, advocacy, and third-person references create lexical ambiguity. Context filters were heuristic.
Several leading signals are redundant: first-person affect, explicit self-state, anxiety, loneliness, low motivation, and clinical disclosure likely share a self-disclosure/activity factor.

caveats: Affective language may describe others, media, jokes, or quoted text; same-post context heuristics are needed.
This signal overlaps strongly with self-state, loneliness, anxiety, and clinical-language features.
findings.evidence_summary: The direction was positive in every fold, with prevalence gaps of 12.4–15.7 percentage points. The rate-based result also persisted, reducing concern that prolific users alone drove it.
findings.prompt_guidance: Prefer user prevalence and per-user hit-post rates over pooled token counts. Combine with persistence and explicit self-state context.

findings.prompt_guidance: Use this as a higher-specificity feature for personal experience, but retain quotation and third-person filters.

quantitative_support.effect: +13.7 percentage points in user prevalence; users with at least three hit posts 18.8% vs 11.2%.

findings.evidence_summary: This was the largest measured association and was stable in every fold, with gaps of 18.8–30.3 percentage points.

quantitative_support.effect: +24.9 percentage points in user prevalence; users with at least three hit posts 40.8% vs 16.8%.

findings.evidence_summary: The direction was positive in all folds, with gaps of 6.4–18.0 percentage points. A broader hopelessness pattern was also consistently higher in diagnosed users, by 2.8–11.2 points.
findings.prompt_guidance: Use as a moderate signal only when paired with first-person context and repetition; avoid interpreting isolated negation or inability phrases clinically.

quantitative_support.effect: +10.3 percentage points in user prevalence; users with at least three hit posts 24.1% vs 14.5%.

findings.evidence_summary: The diagnosed excess persisted in all folds, with gaps of 5.2–13.7 percentage points. Removing posts with heuristic quote, media, joke, news, or advocacy markers still left a positive gap of about 9 percentage points.
findings.prompt_guidance: Keep this as a rare, high-specificity but non-diagnostic feature; apply strict context and third-person checks.

findings.evidence_summary: The combination signal was positive in every fold, though the gap varied substantially from 4.1–17.5 percentage points. Activity-normalized thresholds preserved the same direction.

quantitative_support.effect: +9.0 percentage points in user prevalence; rate threshold of at least 0.5% of posts was met by 3.4% vs 1.6%.

findings.evidence_summary: The disturbance-specific direction was positive in every fold, with gaps of 3.7–15.9 percentage points, but effect size was modest.
findings.prompt_guidance: Use disturbance-specific and first-person patterns; generic sleep frequency is too common to be useful.

quantitative_support.effect: +9.7 percentage points in user prevalence; users with at least three hit posts 4.1% vs 2.1%.
quantitative_support.measure: Specific sleep-disturbance patterns rather than generic sleep or bedtime vocabulary.

caveats: This is a collection, engagement, or exposure confound rather than a clinical signal.
Without timestamps, activity cannot be separated from observation-window duration.
findings.evidence_summary: Diagnosed users had higher median activity in every fold. This makes raw post or token frequency unsuitable as evidence and likely inflates any-user prevalence for common terms.
findings.prompt_guidance: Normalize within user, report user prevalence separately, and consider activity-matched sensitivity analyses.

quantitative_support.control: Median 332 posts and 3,179 words per user.
quantitative_support.diagnosed: Median 386 posts and 3,944.5 words per user.
quantitative_support.effect: Median diagnosed timeline was 54 posts longer; mean was about 96 posts higher. Median word volume was about 766 words higher.

findings.signal: Higher timeline activity among diagnosed users

negative_results: Generic sleep and food vocabulary was widespread and weakly specific: broad sleep prevalence was 95.1% diagnosed vs 91.6% control, and appetite/food vocabulary 86.4% vs 79.7%; only disturbance-specific sleep showed a modest stable gap.
Strict low-energy language was null: 2.4% diagnosed vs 2.3% control, with fold differences ranging from -1.1 to +1.5 percentage points.
Strict anhedonia phrases were rare and not direction-stable across all folds.
Humor, politics/news, and sports were not reliable class markers; humor direction was mixed, politics was near-null, and sports favored control in three of four folds.

Positive affect was not protective: user prevalence was 99.5% diagnosed vs 97.1% control, with higher median post-share among diagnosed users, likely reflecting activity or expressiveness rather than symptom status.
